title: The Gilded Court
tagline: A king inherits a revolution he is not equipped to survive.

scenes.text: Versailles, 1789. The most magnificent palace in the world sits fifteen miles from Paris, where the city's poor are paying half their income for bread. King Louis XVI is not cruel — he is weak. And in a revolution, weakness is fatal.

scenes.speaker: Louis XVI
scenes.text: The treasury is empty. Three wars have bankrupted us. The nobles refuse to be taxed. The people are starving. I don't know what to do. I have never known what to do.

scenes.speaker: Marie Antoinette
scenes.text: They hate me. They call me Madame Deficit, as if I emptied the treasury alone. Louis, you must be strong. You must do something. Anything.

challenge.fact: Louis XVI became king at nineteen on 10 May 1774, when his grandfather Louis XV died of smallpox, inheriting a state close to bankruptcy. He was a skilled locksmith and a passionate map-maker — a careful craftsman in a role that demanded bold political vision.

params.plaintext: THE KING IS DEAD LONG LIVE THE KING

challenge.instruction: Louis remembers May 1774, when a note in the courtiers' grid code ran through Versailles as his grandfather lay dead. Read it — the words that made a nineteen-year-old king.

scenes.text: The French Revolution began not with violence but with fiscal crisis. France was bankrupt from supporting the American Revolution. When Louis XVI called the Estates-General — the first time in 175 years — he unleashed forces he could not control.

challenge.instruction: Once the Estates-General meet, news from Versailles outruns every courier. Plan the line of signal towers the Chappe brothers would soon propose, so that every city of France can see the next one's arms.
challenge.fact: The Palace of Versailles was a machine of political spectacle — every corridor, mirror, and gilded surface designed to awe visitors into submission. Louis XVI inherited this stage but never fully commanded it.

scenes.speaker: Louis XVI
scenes.text: They have voted to become a National Assembly. I told the court it meant nothing. But it means everything. The old world is ending. I can feel it but I cannot stop it.

challenge.instruction: It is July 1789. The Bastille has fallen. Louis XVI needs enough of the Estates behind him to keep his crown — choose the concessions that hold a coalition together.
challenge.fact: Louis XVI was guillotined on 21 January 1793, convicted of treason. His fatal error — the Flight to Varennes in June 1791 — proved to the Revolutionary government that he was conspiring against France with foreign powers.

scenes.text: The circuits of power in Versailles were elaborate — every decision requiring careful switching of alliances and factions. Navigate the political connections that led to the Revolution...

challenge.instruction: When the factions will not obey him, Louis retreats to the one machine he understands: his locksmith's bench. Set the gates so the lock's levers agree with the table on every row.
challenge.fact: Louis XVI kept a locksmith's forge above his private apartments at Versailles and worked there with the locksmith François Gamain. In November 1792 Gamain revealed the hidden iron cupboard, the armoire de fer, that he had helped the king fit in the Tuileries; its papers were used against Louis at his trial.

scenes.speaker: Louis XVI
scenes.text: Two face-down cards: one at Paris, one at St Petersburg. We cannot see who they are until we attack, and an attack reveals every card at the location. The Business War already runs at Paris; you hold a card to start one at St Petersburg.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 5 · Face Down. Win two attacks: fight at Paris where the Business War is running, then carry the fight to St Petersburg by starting your own event there.
challenge.fact: A card on the board can be public (face up) or private (face down). A private card hides its identity and stats from rivals until an attack reveals every card at that location. Your own cards deploy face down; Go Public when being seen helps you.
